batchName: Late Republic: Marius and the Northern Invaders (121-100 BCE) - Medium Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: Marius and the Northern Invaders (121-100 BCE)

questions.question: As tribune of the plebs in 119 BC, what law did Marius pass?
options: He limited consuls to a single term
He narrowed voting walkways to stop the rich peering at ballots
He banned senators from trading overseas
He gave citizenship to all Latin allies
He doubled the state grain ration
questions.explanation: Marius narrowed the walkways where voters cast ballots so the rich could no longer spy on their choices. His career afterwards was bumpy, including a bribery charge that ended in acquittal.
questions.sourceQuote: He passed a law narrowing the walkways where voters cast their ballots, so that the rich could no longer peer at their choices.

questions.question: According to ancient writers, what did a fortune-teller in Utica urge Marius to do?
options: Sacrifice to Neptune before sailing
Beware the ides of March
Marry into the family of Metellus
Trust the gods and test his luck as often as he could
Return to Arpinum and avoid politics
questions.explanation: Ancient writers say the Utica fortune-teller told Marius to trust the gods and test his luck often. He went on to campaign for the consulship from the camp.
questions.sourceQuote: Ancient writers say a fortune-teller in the African city of Utica urged Marius to trust the gods and test his luck as often as he could.

questions.question: How did Marius's army turn the tables after being ambushed near Serif in 106 BC?
options: It held two hills until nightfall, then attacked the enemy camp at dawn
It feigned surrender and struck during the parley
It retreated to the coast and was rescued by the fleet
It formed a hollow square and marched to Cirta
It bribed the Mauretanian king to switch sides mid-battle
questions.explanation: The Romans held two hills until nightfall, then routed the enemy with a dawn surprise attack on their camp. The ambush was led by Jugurtha and his father-in-law, the king of Mauretania.
questions.sourceQuote: The Romans held two hills until nightfall, then routed the enemy with a surprise attack on their camp at dawn.

questions.question: What fatal problem doomed the huge Roman force at Arausio in 105 BC?
options: The two commanders loathed each other and camped on opposite banks
Plague swept through the camp
The army was caught crossing the Alps in winter
Their supply fleet was sunk in a storm
Allied Gauls deserted in the middle of battle
questions.explanation: The commanders camped on opposite banks of the Rhône; one attacked alone and was wiped out, then the other's army was destroyed. Only a few hundred Romans escaped.
questions.sourceQuote: The two commanders loathed each other and camped on opposite banks of the Rhône.

questions.question: What decided the battle against the Teutones near Aquae Sextiae?
options: A downhill charge by the Roman legions
A flood that swept away their wagons
Their allies switching sides
About 3,000 hidden men striking them from behind
A Roman cavalry charge led by Sulla
questions.explanation: As the Teutones charged uphill, about 3,000 Romans hidden nearby hit them from behind. Ancient estimates of the dead and captured ran from 100,000 to 200,000.
questions.sourceQuote: Days later the Teutones charged uphill at the Roman position, only to be hit from behind by about 3,000 men hidden nearby.

questions.question: What stroke of luck gave Marius time to rebuild Rome's army after Arausio?
options: A harsh winter killed most of the Teutones
The Cimbri wandered into Spain instead of marching on Italy
The Cimbri agreed to a truce
The Cimbri's king died suddenly
The Gauls blocked the Alpine passes
questions.explanation: Rather than invading Italy, the Cimbri wandered into Spain, buying Marius precious time. He used it to drill his troops and build a network of spies.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead of marching on Italy, the Cimbri wandered into Spain, giving Marius precious time.

questions.question: What happened to the propertyless volunteers Marius recruited in 107 BC, according to modern specialists?
options: They were enrolled as citizen cavalry
They became Rome's first standing army
They settled permanently in Numidia
They were discharged after the African war
They formed the core of the army at Vercellae
questions.explanation: The 107 BC recruits were discharged after Africa, and the army Marius led against the Cimbri was raised traditionally. Rome kept relying mainly on conscription.
questions.sourceQuote: Those men were discharged after Africa, and the army Marius took over against the Cimbri had been raised in the traditional way.

questions.question: How did Jugurtha set his trap for the Romans near the Muthul River?
options: He bribed their scouts to lead them astray
He lured them into a narrow mountain pass
He cut them off from water and caught them on open desert
He attacked at night with war elephants
He flooded their camp by damming the river
questions.explanation: Jugurtha cut the Romans off from water and caught them in open desert, where his light cavalry had every advantage. The Numidian horsemen broke the army into isolated groups.
questions.sourceQuote: He cut the Romans off from the water they needed and caught them on open desert, where his nimble light cavalry had every advantage.

questions.question: Whose public appeal helped carry Marius's uncertain re-election for 102 BC?
options: Sulla
Catulus
Saturninus
Jugurtha
Metellus
questions.explanation: Saturninus, a young tribune and rabble-rousing champion of the poor, publicly backed Marius. The two later became partners in the bloody year 100 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Re-election for 102 BC was not certain, but a public appeal from Saturninus, a young tribune and rabble-rousing champion of the poor, helped carry him.

questions.question: Some modern historians argue that what, rather than Marius, taught Roman soldiers to turn on fellow Romans?
options: Brutal civil fighting with Italian allies
Service in Hellenistic mercenary armies
Exposure to Gallic customs
The wars against Carthage
The slave revolts in Sicily
questions.explanation: Some historians point to brutal civil fighting with Italian allies instead. Much of the old picture of Marius rests on two moralising ancient critics.
questions.sourceQuote: Some modern historians argue instead that brutal civil fighting with Italian allies, not Marius, taught Roman soldiers to turn their swords on fellow Romans.
